processing: Organic orthodox black tea, sold in grades such as FOP and FBOP. The estate also makes orthodox green tea, and an estate profile mentions decaffeinated, oolong and other specialty teas.
harvest_season: Little is documented about a prized picking; as with other Nilgiri estates, the cool winter months are generally the most valued.
appearance_dry: Orthodox leaf; one FOP/FBOP lot was described as uneven, somewhat broken and twiggy, with a few tightly rolled pieces.
taste_profile: Reviewed FOP/FBOP tea is strongly aromatic, sweet and bready with floral and fruity hints, while the cup itself can be light-bodied and somewhat bitter.

brewing.notes: Western-style. The broken FBOP grade brews faster, so start nearer two and a half minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as a current estate tea by grade, usually without a stated vintage, and often through organic importers. As is usual for Nilgiri black tea, it is best in the first year or two; ask for the picking date where you can. It is not a tea to age.
description:
Korakundah is a very high Nilgiri estate that built its name on organic growing, and its tea is sold by organic tea sellers abroad.

The main product is orthodox black tea in leaf and broken grades, with green tea and smaller specialty lines. Altitude is the usual selling point: cool conditions slow growth, and that tends to give a brighter cup.

One published review found a lovely sweet, floral aroma and a lighter, more bitter cup, so watch the steep time and taste it plain first.

Altitude figures vary: 2,414 metres is the common one, and an estate profile gives an average of about 2,500. Buy on grade and freshness rather than height.
history:
Accounts of the founding are thin: one estate profile says the garden was first opened up in 1930. It is a unit of United Nilgiri Tea Estates, which also owns Devabetta and Chamraj.

It converted to organic methods in 1994 and is described as the first tea estate in South India to be certified organic. It is also promoted as the highest organic tea garden in the world, at 2,414 metres or 7,920 feet.
